claim: The Drosophila larva is composed of 3 thoracic (T1-T3) and nine abdominal segments (A1-A9).
source: The Drosophila larva is composed of 3 thoracic (T1-T3) and nine abdominal segments (A1-A9; Figure 1A), with sensory neurons extending from the periphery into the CNS, and motor neurons extending out of the CNS to innervate body wall muscles.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the larval anatomy.

claim: Most segments contain 30 bilateral body wall muscles that form 'spatial muscle groups' based on common location and orientation.
source: Most segments contain 30 bilateral body wall muscles that form 'spatial muscle groups' based on common location and orientation: dorsal longitudinal (DL; includes previously described DA and some DO muscles), dorsal oblique (DO), ventral longitudinal (VL), ventral oblique (VO), ventral acute (VA) and lateral transverse (LT)(Figure 1B) (Crossley, 1978; Hooper, 1986; Bate, 1990).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with citations to prior work and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Forward crawling behavior in larvae involves a peristaltic contraction wave from posterior to anterior segments.
source: Forward crawling behavior in larvae involves a peristaltic contraction wave from posterior to anterior segments; backward crawling entails a posterior propagation of the contraction wave (Crisp et al., 2008; Dixit et al., 2008; Berni et al., 2012; Gjorgjieva et al., 2013; Heckscher et al., 2015; Pulver et al., 2015; Loveless et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2019) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with multiple citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Backward crawling entails a posterior propagation of the contraction wave.
source: Forward crawling behavior in larvae involves a peristaltic contraction wave from posterior to anterior segments; backward crawling entails a posterior propagation of the contraction wave (Crisp et al., 2008; Dixit et al., 2008; Berni et al., 2012; Gjorgjieva et al., 2013; Heckscher et al., 2015; Pulver et al., 2015; Loveless et al., 2018; Kohsaka et al., 2019) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with multiple citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: There are ~30 bilateral pair of MNs in each segment.
source: There are ~30 bilateral pair of MNs in each segment: 26 pair of type Ib MNs with big boutons that typically innervate one muscle; two pair of type Is MNs with small boutons that innervate large groups of dorsal or ventral muscles; one or two type III insulinergic MNs innervating muscle 12; and three type II ventral unpaired median (VUM) MNs that provide octopaminergic innervation to most muscles (Table 1) (Gorczyca et al., 1993; Landgraf et al., 1997; Hoang and Chiba, 2001; Landgraf et al., 2003; Choi et al., 2004; Mauss et al., 2009; Koon et al., 2011; Koon and Budnik, 2012; Arzan Zarin and Labrador, 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations and reference to Table 1.

claim: Type Ib MNs have big boutons that typically innervate one muscle.
source: There are ~30 bilateral pair of MNs in each segment: 26 pair of type Ib MNs with big boutons that typically innervate one muscle; two pair of type Is MNs with small boutons that innervate large groups of dorsal or ventral muscles; one or two type III insulinergic MNs innervating muscle 12; and three type II ventral unpaired median (VUM) MNs that provide octopaminergic innervation to most muscles (Table 1) (Gorczyca et al., 1993; Landgraf et al., 1997; Hoang and Chiba, 2001; Landgraf et al., 2003; Choi et al., 2004; Mauss et al., 2009; Koon et al., 2011; Koon and Budnik, 2012; Arzan Zarin and Labrador, 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations.

claim: Type Is MNs have small boutons that innervate large groups of dorsal or ventral muscles.
source: There are ~30 bilateral pair of MNs in each segment: 26 pair of type Ib MNs with big boutons that typically innervate one muscle; two pair of type Is MNs with small boutons that innervate large groups of dorsal or ventral muscles; one or two type III insulinergic MNs innervating muscle 12; and three type II ventral unpaired median (VUM) MNs that provide octopaminergic innervation to most muscles (Table 1) (Gorczyca et al., 1993; Landgraf et al., 1997; Hoang and Chiba, 2001; Landgraf et al., 2003; Choi et al., 2004; Mauss et al., 2009; Koon et al., 2011; Koon and Budnik, 2012; Arzan Zarin and Labrador, 2019).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations.

claim: Type Ib MNs innervating muscles in the same spatial muscle group typically project dendrites to the same region of the dorsal neuropil, creating a myotopic map.
source: Elegant pioneering work showed that type Ib MNs innervating muscles in the same spatial muscle group typically project dendrites to the same region of the dorsal neuropil, creating a myotopic map (Landgraf et al., 1997; Mauss et al., 2009).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior work.

claim: All body wall muscles are activated during forward and backward locomotion.
source: Most importantly, all imaged muscles showed a significant rise in GCaMP6f fluorescence during forward and backward locomotion (Figure 2C,F; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 2C,F and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: All MNs and their target muscles are activated during forward and backward locomotion.
source: In addition, because each type Ib MN typically innervates a single muscle, we can use muscle depolarization as a proxy for the activity of its innervating MN. We conclude that all MNs and their target muscles are activated during forward and backward locomotion.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a conclusion based on the muscle activity data and the known innervation pattern.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of mean activity for all observed muscles yields four co-activated muscle groups during forward locomotion (F1–F4).
source: Muscle activity appeared as a continuum with the sequential recruitment of individual muscles, yet hierarchical clustering of the mean activity of each muscle during forward and backward crawling revealed four groups of co-active muscles for both behaviors (Figure 3A–E; Table 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3A-E and Table 2.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of mean activity for all observed muscles yields four co-activated muscle groups during backward locomotion (B1–B4).
source: Muscle activity appeared as a continuum with the sequential recruitment of individual muscles, yet hierarchical clustering of the mean activity of each muscle during forward and backward crawling revealed four groups of co-active muscles for both behaviors (Figure 3A–E; Table 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3A-E and Table 2.

claim: The activation time of each co-activated muscle group was more coherent than the time of their inactivation.
source: The activation time of each co-activated muscle group was more coherent than the time of their inactivation (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3B-E.

claim: Co-activated muscle groups do not fully match previously identified spatial muscle groups.
source: Notably, these co-activated muscle groups do not fully match previously identified spatial muscle groups (compare Figures 1B and 3F,G).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with reference to comparing Figures 1B and 3F,G.

claim: The largest change in recruitment time between forward and backward locomotion was in six muscles: the three muscles in the VO spatial muscle group (muscles 15–17), and muscles 2, 11, and 18.
source: We found that the largest change in recruitment time between forward and backward locomotion was in six muscles: the three muscles in the VO spatial muscle group (muscles 15–17), and muscles 2, 11, and 18 (each in a different spatial muscle group) (Figure 3H,I; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3H,I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The VO spatial muscle group (muscles 15–17) switched from late activity during forward locomotion (F3) to early activity during backward locomotion (B1).
source: The VO spatial muscle group (muscles 15–17) switched from late activity during forward locomotion (F3) to early activity during backward locomotion (B1), whereas the three other neurons switched from early activity during forward locomotion (F1/2) to late activity during backward locomotion (B3/4) (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3H,I.

claim: Muscles 2, 11, and 18 switched from early activity during forward locomotion (F1/2) to late activity during backward locomotion (B3/4).
source: The VO spatial muscle group (muscles 15–17) switched from late activity during forward locomotion (F3) to early activity during backward locomotion (B1), whereas the three other neurons switched from early activity during forward locomotion (F1/2) to late activity during backward locomotion (B3/4) (Figure 3H,I).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3H,I.

claim: Longitudinal muscles tended to be active early and transverse muscles activated late in both forward and backward behaviors.
source: Other spatial muscle groups typically did not change their timing of activation; for example longitudinal muscles tended to be active early and transverse muscles activated late in both behaviors (Figure 3F,G), consistent with prior reports tracking single muscles within each group (Heckscher et al., 2012; Zwart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations and reference to Figure 3F,G.

claim: All differentiated MNs in segment A1 of the newly hatched larval CNS have been successfully identified and reconstructed at single synapse-level resolution.
source: In conclusion, we have successfully identified and reconstructed, at single synapse-level resolution, all differentiated MNs in segment A1 of the newly hatched larval CNS.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a conclusion of the TEM reconstruction work.

claim: All MNs had a dense array of postsynapses on their dendritic projections.
source: We found that all MNs had a dense array of postsynapses on their dendritic projections, but unlike C. elegans (Wen et al., 2012), we observed no presynaptic contacts to other MNs or interneurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unlike C. elegans, Drosophila larval MNs have no presynaptic contacts to other MNs or interneurons.
source: We found that all MNs had a dense array of postsynapses on their dendritic projections, but unlike C. elegans (Wen et al., 2012), we observed no presynaptic contacts to other MNs or interneurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation to C. elegans work and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MNs innervating a single spatial muscle group target their dendrites to a similar region of the neuropil, creating a myotopic map in the neuropil.
source: Motor neurons innervating a single spatial muscle group target their dendrites to a similar region of the neuropil, creating a myotopic map in the neuropil (Landgraf et al., 2003; Mauss et al., 2009).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations to prior work.

claim: MNs in the left and right A1 hemisegments have highly similar postsynapse clustering within the neuropil volume (Pearson correlation coefficient, r = 0.97).
source: To begin, we calculated pairwise synapse similarity scores (Schlegel et al., 2016) for MNs in the left and right A1 hemisegments and observed highly similar postsynapse clustering within the neuropil volume (Pearson correlation coefficient, r = 0.97), which we averaged for subsequent analysis.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with a specific correlation coefficient value and citation.

claim: Unbiased clustering of MNs based on postsynaptic synapse similarity found a highly ordered hierarchical relationship between postsynapse localization and innervation of spatial muscle groups.
source: Next, we performed unbiased clustering of MNs based on postsynaptic synapse similarity, and found a highly ordered hierarchical relationship between postsynapse localization and innervation of spatial muscle groups (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: MNs innervating each spatial muscle group have different postsynaptic distributions along two axes (two sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; p<0.05).
source: We also found that MNs innervating each spatial muscle group have different postsynaptic distributions along two axes (two sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test; p<0.05) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical test results and reference to Figure 5B.

claim: MNs innervating each forward or backward co-active muscle group had distinct postsynapse density maxima along the mediolateral axis.
source: Interestingly, MNs innervating each forward or backward co-active muscle group had distinct postsynapse density maxima along the mediolateral axis, and often along a second axis (either dorsoventral or anterioposterior) (Figure 5C,D arrowheads).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 5C,D.

claim: 118 bilateral PMNs (236 total) with connectivity to A1 MNs were identified.
source: We identified 118 bilateral PMNs (236 total) with connectivity to A1 MNs (Table 3; see Materials and methods for selection criteria).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with reference to Table 3.

claim: PMN presynapses were enriched in the dorsal neuropil.
source: We found that PMN presynapses were enriched in the dorsal neuropil, as expected, and PMN postsynapses were distributed throughout the neuropil (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 6A,B.

claim: PMN postsynapses were distributed throughout the neuropil.
source: We found that PMN presynapses were enriched in the dorsal neuropil, as expected, and PMN postsynapses were distributed throughout the neuropil (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 6A,B.

claim: Each PMN synapsed with an average of 8.0 MNs.
source: Each PMN synapsed with an average of 8.0 MNs (Figure 6C), while each MN received input from an average of 32.5 PMNs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 6C.

claim: Each MN received input from an average of 32.5 PMNs.
source: Each PMN synapsed with an average of 8.0 MNs (Figure 6C), while each MN received input from an average of 32.5 PMNs (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 6D.

claim: PMNs made 7495 synapses on A1 MNs, which accounted for 12.7% of PMN output and 76% of the total A1 MN input.
source: PMNs made 7495 synapses on A1 MNs, which accounted for 12.7% of PMN output and 76% of the total A1 MN input (excluding A2 MN-25) (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with specific numbers and reference to Figure 6E,F.

claim: MNs received 59.6% to 97.9% of their total inputs from the 118 PMN pairs.
source: Conversely, MNs received 59.6% to 97.9% of their total inputs from these 118 PMN pairs (excluding RP3 which has most of its postsynapses anterior to A1) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with specific percentages and reference to Figure 6F.

claim: Most PMNs projected contralaterally.
source: In addition, most PMNs projected contralaterally, had local arbors, and had postsynaptic inputs on their more proximal processes (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 6G-I.

claim: 30 of the 118 PMNs innervated MNs in a single spatial muscle group.
source: We found that 30 of the 118 PMNs innervated MNs in a single spatial muscle group (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 7D.

claim: A similar number of PMNs innervated MNs in a single co-active muscle group.
source: Interestingly, a similar numbers of PMNs innervated MNs in a single co-active muscle group (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 7E,F.

claim: The majority of PMNs innervate MNs in multiple spatial or co-active muscle groups.
source: Thus, we have identified groups of PMNs that specifically innervate co-active MNs, consistent with a 'labeled line' model for generating motor output, yet we note that the majority of PMNs innervate MNs in multiple spatial or co-active muscle groups.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the connectivity analysis.

claim: All PMNs innervate multiple MNs, and there is no evidence for specific PMNs innervating specific MNs, whether they are differentially recruited or not.
source: We found that all PMNs innervate multiple MNs, and there is no evidence for specific PMNs innervating specific MNs, whether they are differentially recruited or not (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 7G.

claim: PMN combinatorial coding is likely to generate the observed MN differential recruitment during forward and backward locomotion.
source: We conclude that PMN combinatorial coding is likely to generate the observed MN differential recruitment during forward and backward locomotion.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The PMN A27h is strongly connected to MNs in co-active group F3.
source: We found that the PMN A27h (Figure 7H) is strongly connected to MNs in co-active group F3 (Figure 7H'), so we asked whether A27h was recruited after the U1-U5 MNs in co-active groups F1/F2.
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 7H and 7H'.

claim: Dual color calcium imaging showed that the F1/F2 MNs were active prior to the F3 PMN A27h.
source: Indeed, dual color calcium imaging showed that the F1/F2 MNs were active prior to the F3 PMN A27h (Figure 7H'').
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 7H''.

claim: MN18 is highly asymmetric.
source: We examined the morphology of differentially recruited MNs and found that MN18, but not the others, is highly asymmetric (Figure 8A–E).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 8A-E.

claim: The asymmetric distribution of postsynaptic sites on MN18 should lead to its earlier activation during forward than backward locomotion.
source: The asymmetric distribution of postsynaptic sites on MN18 should lead to its earlier activation during forward than backward locomotion. This is consistent with its activity pattern deciphered using muscle calcium imaging during these behaviors (Figure 3).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a prediction based on morphology and confirmed by reference to Figure 3.

claim: A02i and A03a4 have axons extending 1–2 segments anterior of the dendrites.
source: For example, A02i and A03a4 have axons extending 1–2 segments anterior of the dendrites; A03a5 has axons projecting 1–2 segments posterior of the dendrites; whereas A03g is a symmetric PMN (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 8F-H.

claim: A03a5 has axons projecting 1–2 segments posterior of the dendrites.
source: For example, A02i and A03a4 have axons extending 1–2 segments anterior of the dendrites; A03a5 has axons projecting 1–2 segments posterior of the dendrites; whereas A03g is a symmetric PMN (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 8F-H.

claim: A03g is a symmetric PMN.
source: For example, A02i and A03a4 have axons extending 1–2 segments anterior of the dendrites; A03a5 has axons projecting 1–2 segments posterior of the dendrites; whereas A03g is a symmetric PMN (Figure 8F–H).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 8F-H.

claim: The asymmetric PMNs are likely to contribute to the differential MN/muscle recruitment in forward and backward locomotion.
source: Due to the opposite direction of wave propagation in backward and forward locomotion, the asymmetric PMNs are likely to contribute to the differential MN/muscle recruitment in forward and backward locomotion.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as an inference based on the asymmetric morphology and wave propagation direction.

claim: The reconstructed PMN connectome is capable of producing the observed timing of MN/muscle activation.
source: To assess whether the reconstructed PMN connectome is capable of producing the observed timing of MN/muscle activation, we developed a recurrent network model of two adjacent segments.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as the goal of the modeling work.

claim: The observed connections among PMNs within a segment are sufficient to generate appropriately timed MN activity for forward and backward behaviors.
source: We found that, although the connectivity among PMNs within a segment is sparse (roughly 7% of all possible pairwise connections), the observed connections are nonetheless sufficient to generate appropriately timed MN activity for the two distinct behaviors (Figure 9A,B; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 9A,B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The connectivity among PMNs within a segment is sparse (roughly 7% of all possible pairwise connections).
source: We found that, although the connectivity among PMNs within a segment is sparse (roughly 7% of all possible pairwise connections), the observed connections are nonetheless sufficient to generate appropriately timed MN activity for the two distinct behaviors (Figure 9A,B; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with a specific percentage.

claim: In the models, distinct sequences of PMN activity for forward and backward locomotion tile the period of time over which MNs are active.
source: In the models, distinct sequences of PMN activity for forward and backward locomotion tile the period of time over which MNs are active (Figure 9C; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 9C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PMN A14a is active during co-activated muscle group F1.
source: In our model, the PMN A14a is active at F1 and is inactive at F4 (Figure 9C). Similarly, experimental data show that A14a is inhibitory and is active during co-activated muscle group F1; and blocking A14a activity removes the contraction delay between muscles in co-activated muscle group F1 and F4 (Zwart et al., 2016), thereby validating our model.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation and reference to Figure 9C.

claim: Blocking A14a activity removes the contraction delay between muscles in co-activated muscle group F1 and F4.
source: In our model, the PMN A14a is active at F1 and is inactive at F4 (Figure 9C). Similarly, experimental data show that A14a is inhibitory and is active during co-activated muscle group F1; and blocking A14a activity removes the contraction delay between muscles in co-activated muscle group F1 and F4 (Zwart et al., 2016), thereby validating our model.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation.

claim: The PMNs A18b3 and A18a are both active during forward locomotion, but only A18a is active during backward locomotion.
source: In our model, the PMNs A18b3 and A18a are both active during forward locomotion, but only A18a is active during backward locomotion (Figure 9C). Experimental data show that A18a and A18b3 are active precisely as proposed in our model (Hasegawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation and reference to Figure 9C.

claim: The cholinergic A18j and A01c PMNs are active at F4.
source: Furthermore, our model predicts the cholinergic A18j and A01c PMNs are active at F4, which is supported by experimental data on these neurons (where they were called eIN1,2; Zwart et al., 2016).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model prediction supported by cited experimental data.

claim: The A31k activity peak coincides with a decline of activity in MNs innervating early co-activated muscle groups during both forward and backward locomotion.
source: Dual color calcium imaging data revealed that the A31k activity peak coincides with a decline of activity in MNs innervating early co-activated muscle groups during both forward and backward locomotion (Figure 10A,B), further validating our model.
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 10A,B.

claim: A31k and A06l showed concurrent, rhythmic activity during forward and backward locomotion.
source: We expressed GCaMP6m in both neurons, which we could distinguish based on their different axon projections, and found that they showed concurrent, rhythmic activity (Figure 10C,D), and thus both neurons show a delayed activation relative to MNs.
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 10C,D.

claim: A23a was active earlier during backward locomotion than forward locomotion.
source: Our model predicts that A23a was active earlier during backward locomotion than forward locomotion (Figure 9C). We expressed GCaMP6m in a subset of MNs and jRCaMP1b in A23a, and validated the prediction of our model (Figure 10E,F).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a model prediction that was validated, with reference to Figure 9C and Figure 10E,F.

claim: A model lacking complex single-neuron dynamics such as post-inhibitory rebound or spike-frequency adaptation is sufficient to produce the observed motor pattern.
source: It is also notable that a model lacking complex single-neuron dynamics such as post-inhibitory rebound or spike-frequency adaptation, which are critical for modeling other central pattern generator circuits (Marder and Bucher, 2001), is sufficient to produce the observed motor pattern.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation.

claim: All imaged larval body wall muscles are bifunctional and are activated during both forward and backward locomotion.
source: Our single-muscle calcium imaging data indicate that all imaged larval body wall muscles are bifunctional and are activated during both forward and backward locomotion.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a conclusion from the calcium imaging data.

claim: The forward-specific excitatory PMN A27h connects to another forward-specific excitatory PMN A18b3 innervating F1-F2 MNs.
source: The previously described forward-specific excitatory PMN A27h (Fushiki et al., 2016; Carreira-Rosario et al., 2018), with F3 onset, connects to another forward-specific excitatory PMN A18b3 (Hasegawa et al., 2016) innervating F1-F2 MNs.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations.

claim: When A27h activates F3, it also maintains activity of A18b3 to ensure continued excitation of F1/F2 MNs.
source: Thus, when A27h activates F3, it also maintains activity of A18b3 to ensure continued excitation of F1/F2 MNs (Figure 11A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 11A.

claim: A27h excites PMN A18b3 in the next anterior segment, which could advance the intersegmental forward contraction wave.
source: A27h also excites PMN A18b3 in the next anterior segment, which could advance the intersegmental forward contraction wave; similarly, A18b3 excites two inhibitory PMNs (A06c, A14a) in the next anterior segment which may prevent premature activation of F3/4 MNs (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 11B.

claim: A18b3 excites two inhibitory PMNs (A06c, A14a) in the next anterior segment which may prevent premature activation of F3/4 MNs.
source: A27h also excites PMN A18b3 in the next anterior segment, which could advance the intersegmental forward contraction wave; similarly, A18b3 excites two inhibitory PMNs (A06c, A14a) in the next anterior segment which may prevent premature activation of F3/4 MNs (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 11B.

claim: A14a disinhibits F1/F2 MNs via silencing A02e PMN.
source: Moreover, consistent with F1/F2 vs F3/F4 temporal segregation, A14a disinhibits F1/F2 MNs via silencing A02e PMN (Figure 11B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 11B.

claim: The backward-specific PMN A27k excites B4 MNs as well as the inhibitory PMNs A02e and A02g innervating B1/B2.
source: Next, we examined circuit motifs composed of a backward-specific PMN, A27k (also known as ifb-BWD) (Kohsaka et al., 2019). A27k excites B4 MNs as well as the inhibitory PMNs A02e and A02g innervating B1/B2.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation.

claim: A27k synapses in the next anterior segment with the excitatory neurons A01c1, A01c2, and A18j (innervating B4), as well as with the inhibitory PMN A02e innervating B1/B2.
source: A27k also synapses in the next anterior segment with the excitatory neurons A01c1, A01c2, and A18j (innervating B4), as well as with the inhibitory PMN A02e innervating B1/B2.
evidence: This is explicitly stated.

claim: The TEM volume is for an L1 newly hatched larva.
source: The TEM volume is for an L1 newly hatched larva (Ohyama et al., 2015), and is available by request from Albert Cardona (Cambridge University).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation.

claim: The 118 PMNs were selected if they had presynapses to greater than 1% of a MN postsynapse population and greater than four total synapses.
source: The 118 PMNs were selected if they had presynapses to greater than 1% of a MN postsynapse population and greater than four total synapses (left+right combined).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a selection criterion.

claim: An isolated CNS without sensory input (including no proprioception) can maintain forward and backward waves of motor neuron activity.
source: Prior studies of C. elegans have highlighted the importance of proprioception in order to drive locomotion (Kunert et al., 2017), while our model does not require proprioceptive input to generate the observed motor pattern, consistent with data showing that an isolated CNS without sensory input (including no proprioception) can maintain forward and backward waves of motor neuron activity (Pulver et al., 2015).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citations.
